Stage 3 · Grammar

Getting the question right

One word order for almost everything — and one exception worth knowing.

Read these four questions.
  • What made you move abroad?
  • How long have you been living there?
  • Who taught you to do that?
  • What’s it like to start again at forty?
Some of these have no auxiliary verb (do, did, have, is). Which ones?
One question type in English breaks the inversion rule — and it is the one learners get wrong.

The basic rule for English questions is inversion: the auxiliary verb moves in front of the subject. You have finished becomes Have you finished? Where there is no auxiliary, as in the present and past simple, English supplies one — do, does or did — and the main verb then returns to its base form: Did you go?, never Did you went?

There is one systematic exception, and it accounts for a large share of B1 question errors. When the question word is itself the subject of the sentence — when it replaces the person or thing doing the action — there is no inversion and no auxiliary at all. Who wrote this report? and What happened? are complete and correct. Adding did (Who did write this?) turns them into something else entirely.

The contrast between subject and object questions is not just a formal detail; it changes meaning. Who called you? asks who did the calling. Who did you call? asks whom you called. The only visible difference is the presence of did, and getting it wrong reverses the question.

Beyond accuracy, the type of question you ask shapes the answer you get, which matters in the interview context of this lesson. A yes/no question closes a conversation down; a wh- question opens it up; a tag question checks something you already believe. An interviewer who only asks yes/no questions learns nothing, however grammatical the questions are.

Before you look at the table: the tables below run through the question forms tense by tense, then set subject questions against object questions. That last pair is the one to study hardest.
The normal order, tense by tense

The exception: subject questions

The testthe answer is the object: I admire her.the answer is the subject: She taught me.

One test for subject questions. Answer the question. If the answer goes at the front of the sentence, the question needed no do, does or did: Who taught you? — My father taught me.

Everything else keeps the same shape. Question word, then auxiliary, then subject, then verb. The tense changes; the order does not.

The mistake to avoid. Do not use the statement order in a question: not Where you are from? but Where are you from? This is the single most noticeable error at this level.

And the opposite mistake. Do not add an auxiliary to a subject question: not Who did write it? but Who wrote it? — unless you are expressing surprise.

Full grammar reference — question forms — including subject and object questions

What it is

A full map of how English builds questions. The core rule is inversion: the auxiliary comes before the subject. Where there is no auxiliary, the present or past simple supplies do / does / did. The one systematic exception is the subject question, where the question word is itself the subject and no inversion happens at all.

What it means, and what it does

Word order in questions is where B1 learners are most often understood but marked wrong. Beyond accuracy, the type of question shapes the answer you get: a yes/no question closes the conversation, a wh- question opens it, and a tag question checks something you already believe. An interviewer who only asks yes/no questions gets nothing; that is the practical point of this lesson.

When and why we use it

The basic rule for English questions is inversion: the auxiliary verb moves in front of the subject. You have finished becomes Have you finished? Where there is no auxiliary, as in the present and past simple, English supplies one — do, does or did — and the main verb then returns to its base form: Did you go?, never Did you went?

There is one systematic exception, and it accounts for a large share of B1 question errors. When the question word is itself the subject of the sentence — when it replaces the person or thing doing the action — there is no inversion and no auxiliary at all. Who wrote this report? and What happened? are complete and correct. Adding did (Who did write this?) turns them into something else entirely.

The contrast between subject and object questions is not just a formal detail; it changes meaning. Who called you? asks who did the calling. Who did you call? asks whom you called. The only visible difference is the presence of did, and getting it wrong reverses the question.

Beyond accuracy, the type of question you ask shapes the answer you get, which matters in the interview context of this lesson. A yes/no question closes a conversation down; a wh- question opens it up; a tag question checks something you already believe. An interviewer who only asks yes/no questions learns nothing, however grammatical the questions are.

Typical situations

You need these forms for interviews in both directions, for getting information from colleagues and services, for checking facts, and for keeping any conversation going.

  • Asking for confirmation — yes/no questions, answered with a short answer.Did you enjoy working abroad?
  • Asking for information — wh- questions: what, where, when, why, how, which, whose.What made you decide to move?
  • Asking who or what did something — subject questions — no do / does / did.Who taught you to design gardens?
  • Checking something you expect to be true — tag questions.You’re currently working in Luanda, aren’t you?
  • Asking about degree or quantity — how + adjective or adverb.How long have you been there?
  • Asking politely or indirectly — the embedded form from Lesson 12.Could you tell me what attracted you to the job?
  • Asking for a description or opinion — fixed patterns worth learning whole.What’s it like to live there? · What do you think of the working conditions?

How it differs from similar structures

Who called you? (subject — who did the calling) · Who did you call? (object — whom you called). The presence of did is the only signal, and it changes the meaning completely.
What is he like? = describe his character · What does he like? = what does he enjoy · What does he look like? = describe his appearance.

How to build it

Yes/no: auxiliary + subject + base verb?
Wh- object question: wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base verb?
Wh- subject question: wh-word + verb + …?  (no auxiliary, no inversion)
Tag: statement, + opposite auxiliary + pronoun?
Present simpleDo you work here? · Does she supervise anyone?
Past simpleDid you apply? · When did you move?
Present continuousAre you working today? · What are you doing?
Present perfectHave you ever worked abroad? · How long have you been there?
ModalsCan you supervise a team? · Would you move again?
be as the main verbAre you happy there? — be inverts on its own, with no do.
Subject questionWho designed this? · What happened? — note: no did.
Object questionWho did you meet? · What did you design?
Negative questionDon’t you like it? · Aren’t you coming?
Tag questionsYou work here, don’t you? · She isn’t coming, is she?

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • Yes/no questions normally take rising intonation; wh- questions take falling intonation. A wh- question said with a rise sounds surprised or unsure.
  • A tag with a falling tone is checking something you already believe; with a rising tone it is a genuine question.
  • Did you is usually reduced to /dʹə/ and What do you to /wɒdjə/ in fast speech — the auxiliary is there, just weak.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The subject question is the rule to master. If the question word replaces the person or thing doing the action, use no auxiliary and keep statement order: Who wrote this? If it replaces the object, the auxiliary returns: Who did you write to?
  • After do / does / did the main verb is always the base form: Did you go?, never Did you went?
  • What… like? asks for a description; How…? asks about health or a process; What…? alone asks for identity. What’s she like? (character) vs How is she? (health) vs What does she look like? (appearance).
  • Prepositions normally stay at the end in questions: Who did you speak to? Moving it to the front (To whom did you speak?) is formal and requires whom.
  • Tag questions reverse the polarity: a positive statement takes a negative tag and vice versa. With I am, the tag is irregular: I’m late, aren’t I?
  • A negative question often expresses surprise or invites agreement rather than asking for information: Don’t you want the job?

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Who did write this report? → Who wrote this report?In a subject question there is no auxiliary.
  • Where you did work before? → Where did you work before?Only the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.
  • Did you went to the interview? → Did you go to the interview?After did, the base form.
  • How long you have been there? → How long have you been there?The auxiliary must come before the subject.
  • What means this word? → What does this word mean?What here is the object, so the auxiliary is needed.
  • You are from Portugal, isn’t it? → You’re from Portugal, aren’t you?The tag repeats the auxiliary and the subject of the statement.

More examples in context

  • yes/noDid you get sick pay in that job?
  • wh- objectWhat did the company offer besides the salary?
  • subject questionWho persuaded you to apply?
  • subject questionWhat happened to the original team?
  • present perfectHow long have you been working in Luanda?
  • modalWould you move abroad again for a better salary?
  • descriptionWhat’s it like being the only foreigner in the office?
  • tag, checkingYou retrained as a landscape designer, didn’t you?
  • negative questionDon’t you miss Athens at all?
  • indirectCould you tell me what attracted you to the position?

A tip for remembering it

Ask one question before you build the question: does the question word do the action? If yes — Who called? What happened? — leave the auxiliary out. If no, put the auxiliary straight after the question word and the base verb after the subject. Everything else in this lesson follows from that single test.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Questions invert the auxiliary and the subject: Have you…? Did she…?
  2. In the present and past simple, do / does / did supplies the auxiliary and the main verb stays in the base form.
  3. Subject questions take no auxiliary: Who wrote it? Object questions do: Who did you write to?
  4. Be as a main verb inverts on its own, with no do.
  5. Prepositions normally stay at the end of the question.
  6. Tags reverse the polarity and repeat the auxiliary; I’m…, aren’t I? is the irregular one.
